en: Then, considering their own office to be extremely difficult to fulfill,
those who desire victory— such as teachers and others— should strive for self-mastery.
Then, for one who has conquered the senses, self-possession and the state of being a yogi become possible;
through the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma) and other disciplines, the mastery of the senses is gradually attained.

Breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), contemplation (vīkṣaṇa), recitation (japa), and absorption (samādhi) are the limbs; yoga itself is the eighth, the possessor of these limbs.
Prāṇa is the wind that has risen in the east; its extension is perspiration.
Characterized by impelling, drawing, and restraint, it removes defects of the sacrificial rite.
Then, once their minds have become habituated to tasting even a small fragment of pleasure,
the withdrawal of the senses must be performed— the turning away from everything.
Therefore, when the contact with the objects of the senses has ceased, the consciousness of the mind attains the fitness for concentration upon a state conceived according to one's own will.
Meditation is contemplation directed toward that object, and that is prescribed again and again; when it attains one-pointedness, it is established as *samādhi*.
O Sage, recitation is the verbal expression of that [mantra]; meditation is the bringing of the object of focus before one's eyes;
and investigation is the observation of the object immediately following the conceptualization of its nature. (MT 4.8)
When one knows the state to be abandoned and that which is to be adopted from its stability,
as well as what nourishes that [state] and its supreme adversary which nourishes that [abandonment].
For the yogin who has exerted effort regarding these [powers], both individually and collectively,
his powers shine forth pervading the universe, like the rays of the sun.
No man— neither a Rākṣasa, a Dānava, nor a human—
is able to overcome him as he shines intensely with the radiance of his vision, action, and vital breath.
The cause of the mind's withdrawal is the exhaustion of the vital breath through sensory contact;
this withdrawal is the root of concentration (dhāraṇā) and the rest, and therefore it is the foundation of everything.
O best of gods, please explain in detail that which is remote and established, as well as whatever other means there may be for the accomplishment of yoga.
It is not possible to explain this in detail for fear of prolixity regarding the procedure; nevertheless, a brief summary is stated here because the question must necessarily be answered.
Having discharged urine and so forth according to the rule, one should cleanse the penis, the anus, the left hand, and both hands with one, half, ten, and seven applications of earth respectively.
Having drunk water twice while observing the vow, and having wiped his mouth three times,
he should touch his arms, navel, and heart twice or thrice, once his lower lip has been purified.

One who is healthy, having eaten wholesome and digested food, should sit upon a comfortable seat facing north in a house enclosed by three walls or in a forest and similar place free from disturbances. MT 4.17.
Having paid homage to Maheśāna, Umā, Skanda, and the lords of the Gaṇas,
with his neck, head, and chest held straight, he fixed both his eyes upon the tip of his nose.
Protecting the testicles with his heels, not allowing his teeth to touch one another,
with his body firmly rooted and his tongue held against the tip of his upper teeth, he remains well-established.
One should exhale the breath through a single cycle until it reaches the limit of one's power;
that is the *recaka*, and through its practice, [one becomes capable] in actions involving piercing and dispersing.
Gradually, it attains power even over distant objects;
through the external air, the limit of the capacity of the embodied form is filled.
Through that practice, inhalation (pūraka) can draw in even what is very heavy;
abandoning both exhalation and inhalation, retention (nirodha) is known as the "pot-like breath" (kumbhaka).
Through the practice of that, the power of obstruction attains unimpeded manifestation;
likewise for this wise one as he moves along the paths of the Moon, the Sun, and the Lord.
Having realized his fitness for that dharma, the yogi should accomplish the intended goal;
he should practice inhalation or retention while the breath remains on the path of the moon.

For the sake of nourishment, victory over death, and so forth—for oneself or another—one should perform exhalation (*recaka*) when there is no fire blazing, when a tree is withering, or when seeds are being destroyed. (MT 4.25)
However, one should perform exhalation (recaka) during instances such as when afflicted by demonic possession, insanity, or the onset of poison;
and during meditation, worship, recitation, and the like, as well as at the time of casting off the body for the sake of Śiva.
Kumbhaka and recaka are prescribed for the establishment of initiation;
they are classified as minor, middling, and superior according to twelve *tāla*s and so forth.
The palm tree has twelve circumferences equal to the girth of the knees;
it is endowed with meditation and recitation, while the other is "with seed" (sagarbha), yet devoid of those qualities.
Just as one who is pregnant is not [able to act] for the sake of mental stability, so it is with others;
[specifically,] the sin committed at night is [cleansed] at dawn, and that committed during the day at the end of the day.
Even without an embryo, he destroys the instability of the gods as they rush about;
he becomes one who has bathed in sacred fords and is initiated into all sacrifices.

He who would constantly act as a vessel for his ancestors should practice this meditation together with its womb; he should meditate upon the God who has gone beyond the darkness of the path and always recite that which expresses Him.

Furthermore, the principles (tattvas) such as earth and the rest, or those governed by their respective forms, cannot be established as non-conscious principles that are capable of providing assistance. (MT 4.32)
Therefore, one should meditate on the body as being Śiva for the sake of accomplishing whatever is desired,
as well as the concentrations (dhāraṇā), the mental states (vṛtti), and the vital breath (anila).
The wise one, with an undistracted mind and having established mental composure, should practice the *sagarbha* breath-retention (*kumbhaka*) for a duration equal to the qualities of the sun.
It receives the name "dhāraṇā" (retention) because it bestows the perfection of retention;
the word *dhāraṇā* has the sense of "staying," and it also has the sense of "abiding" by way of metaphorical usage.
These [qualities], beginning with barley-color (yavanya) and so forth, are the abodes of the first [type of person], and not of the other;
they are, by their form, like gold, snow, light, and black, yet transparent.
The forms of the altar, the half-moon, the triangle, the circle,
and the lotus are for the sake of attaining stability, nourishment, incineration, impulsion, and emptiness, respectively.
Having understood that they are accompanied by the void of the vajra-flame drop,
one should recognize them as being either obstructive, conforming, or neutral.
For the sake of attaining the desired goal, the yogi should maintain these [elements] both individually and collectively.
In which location should the wise one contemplate the form of concentration?
Furthermore, O Lord of the Gods, tell me the fruit of these [elements] both individually and collectively:
how one who knows the goal should maintain the earth when the heart and mind are distracted.
One who is thirsty [should place] water in the throat; when the digestive fire in the stomach is weak, [one should place] fire there;
and for the sake of establishing the functions of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth, one should place air in the heart, the throat, and other locations.
When they are overcome by poison and the like, space is useful among them;
likewise, among all beings, space, water, wind, fire, and earth [are useful].
Water and fire, earth and wind, water and earth, and fire and wind; these are the neutral, enemy, and friendly planets respectively, arranged in pairs within each of the four quadrants.
Having understood this, the wise person should apply themselves for the sake of attaining their desired goal.
What are the locations within this little body for the functions of the vital breaths and so forth?
O best of gods, tell me what would happen once those [energies] have been conquered;
for by fixing [the mind] upon his heart, navel, chest, throat, and back, [he attains mastery]. (MT 4.45)
The yogin shall attain mastery over the functions such as inhalation and the rest;
having conquered his vital breaths, he assumes a body for himself according to his own will.
One who has conquered the removal of [impurities] eats, yet does not discharge excrement and the like;
one who has conquered the upward movement attains qualities such as mastery over speech.

Through victory over the equalized functions, one becomes free from decay and a master of oneself; through mastery over the body and its movements, there shall be power over the bending [of the body] once it has been conquered.
Non-attachment to mud, water, and thorns; inexhaustible and marvelous vigor;
the twelve dhāraṇīs; and meditative absorption that grants the manifestation of divine light.

Concentration is the cause of the eight powers, beginning with *aṇiman*; these twelve [qualities] are attained even without breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), provided one remains established in the mind with a self-subdued nature.
By practicing these together, one immediately attains the qualities mentioned [in the preceding verses];
whatever object one undertakes, it is accomplished through the application of the sequence as prescribed.
"In each and every case, his manifestation of consciousness shall have that pervasion as its object"—
having thus reflected with his own eye upon everything established externally.
Having renounced all objective entities, one should practice the reality of Śiva (śivatattva),
even performing breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and other disciplines while remaining established within the womb of Śiva.
The living being who gives up their life attains the state of Śiva;
for the supreme form of Maheśvara can never be fully conceptualized through meditation.
Since that which is imagined due to diversity leads to delusion, how could the mind find stability therein?
At that time, neither the earth nor the water element, despite their variegated marks, should be the object of meditation or concentration.
Nevertheless, it is heard that yogins have achieved mastery in those two through practice;
how, however, can there be stability of mind for one whose mind is distracted by enjoyments?
Hara did not intend this means of attainment for those beings who are not yet dispassionate;
even the entire world can be gradually made an object of meditation.
What wonder is there in a body subdued by those who possess the practice of dispassion? Or what measure can be assigned to the form of one who is a yogi established in the substrate of all?
Having mentally conceptualized the locations, forms, and dimensions of all beings at all times as being benefactors in every way, [one should practice]. (MT 4.59)
Whatever object the mind finds rest in, that should be meditated upon again and again;
by means of that, stability of this mind, characterized by distinguished qualities, arises gradually.
For one who acts correctly in this way, without even the conceptualization of forms, the purification of yoga arises once obstacles have been destroyed. (MT 4.61)
For one who thinks of nothing, his own true form unfolds—
the form that perceives and acts upon all objects, which is blissful and imperishable.
That which, once attained, one does not again encounter the union with suffering that brings inauspiciousness—
this is the secret of all secrets, praised by the Siddhas and the immortals.
Direct vision of Śambhu is supremely purifying and most excellent;

it should not be given to one who has resided [in the lineage] for only a short time, nor to one who is overly negligent, nor to one who lacks intelligence, nor to one who lacks austerity, nor to one who does not worship Śiva.
Through the practice of this, shining brilliantly with nets of rays from his divine accomplishments, he wanders through the desired worlds;
then, at the proper time, having cast off the body along with its outflows, he abides in his own self as the dwelling place of wondrous conduct.
